stem: A CI system authenticates tens of thousands of short pipeline jobs per hour. Each job reads a few secrets and finishes in minutes, and nothing needs to renew, revoke or create child tokens. Which token type reduces storage load on Vault the most?

choices.text: Batch tokens, because they are encrypted blobs that need no storage writes when they are created.
Root tokens with a use limit, because root tokens bypass the token store when they are generated.
Service tokens with a short TTL, because Vault removes their storage entries immediately after the last use.
Periodic service tokens, because the fixed period lets Vault skip tracking each token in its token store.

stem: Which statement about batch tokens, compared with service tokens, is accurate?

choices.text: A batch token can create child tokens, which expire together with it.
A batch token can be revoked early by looking up its accessor and revoking that accessor.
A batch token is always issued with a fixed TTL and cannot be renewed to extend it.
A batch token can be created as periodic when the role sets a period value.

stem: An application obtained a token with `vault token create -type=batch -ttl=15m`. After ten minutes it runs `vault token renew` and gets an error. What explains the failure?

choices.text: The application first has to call the renewal endpoint with the accessor, which batch tokens return at creation.
Batch tokens can only be renewed after the first half of the TTL has passed, and ten minutes is too early.
The token must be created with the `-period` flag before Vault will accept renewals for it.
Batch tokens are not renewable, so the application must request a new token before the TTL ends.

stem: A platform team runs Vault with performance replication and wants orphan tokens that clients can use against any performance cluster. Which choice fits, and what is the trade-off?

choices.text: Root tokens, accepting that they need a quorum of unseal key holders for every creation.
Batch orphan tokens, accepting that they cannot be renewed or revoked individually.
Periodic service tokens, accepting that the period must be identical on every cluster.
Service tokens, accepting that they are written to storage on every cluster that serves the client.

stem: A release pipeline creates one token per deployment for a deploy agent. The agent must be able to start a helper process that gets its own sub-token, and an operator wants to revoke the agent's access mid-run if needed. Which token fits?

choices.text: A recovery token, because it is the only type meant for short-lived automation.
A service token, because it can create child tokens and can be revoked before it expires.
A batch token with `-orphan`, because orphan batch tokens can create their own children.
A batch token, because an operator can revoke it on its own with `vault token revoke`.

stem: A new administrator asks what makes a root token different from the other tokens a Vault cluster issues. Which statement about root tokens is accurate?

choices.text: A root token has the `root` policy attached and is the only token that can be set to never expire.
A root token always has a 32 day TTL so that a forgotten one revokes itself.
A root token can be created by any token whose policy grants `create` on `auth/token/create`.
A root token is a batch token with an added `root` policy, so it needs no storage.

stem: Which TWO of the following are documented ways to create a root token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enabling the `userpass` auth method and assigning the `root` policy to a user.
Running `vault token create -policy=root` with a token that has the `default` policy.
Running `vault login -method=token` with any token that has `sudo` on `auth/token/create`.
Running `vault operator init`, which prints the initial root token.
Running `vault operator generate-root` with a quorum of unseal key holders.

stem: All operators lost the root token, and the production cluster is healthy and unsealed. Which action produces a new root token without restarting Vault?

choices.text: Run `vault token create -policy=root` using any token that has the `admin` policy attached to it.
Run `vault operator init` again so that Vault prints a brand new initial root token for the team.
Start it with `vault operator generate-root -init`, then have key holders submit shares up to the threshold.
Restart the nodes in dev mode so that Vault creates a fresh root token on every startup.

stem: During `vault operator generate-root`, the team passes `-otp=<value>` when they start the attempt. What is the OTP for?

choices.text: It authenticates each unseal key holder, so only people with that code can submit key shares.
It replaces the unseal key threshold, so a single holder can finish the attempt with the OTP.
The final root token is XORed with it, so you recover the real token with `-decode` and the same OTP.
It sets how many seconds the new root token stays valid before it is revoked automatically.

stem: Which practice best matches HashiCorp's guidance for root tokens in a production cluster?

choices.text: Use a root token only for initial setup or emergencies, then revoke it and generate a new one later if needed.
Give the root token a short TTL and renew it automatically from a scheduled job.
Keep one root token for each administrator so audit logs can tell users apart.
Store the initial root token in a shared secret store so any on-call engineer can use it daily.

stem: An admin finishes initial setup using the root token and wants to remove it. Which command revokes the root token currently set in `VAULT_TOKEN`?

choices.text: `vault token renew -increment=0`
`vault operator generate-root -cancel`
`vault operator seal`
`vault token revoke -self`

stem: An auditor sees that every `vault token create` response includes both a `token` and a `token_accessor` field. What is a token accessor?

choices.text: The policy name that Vault attaches to a token so that it can read its own details.
A reference returned at token creation that allows limited actions on the token without exposing its ID.
A second secret that must be sent together with the token to authenticate on every request.
A hash of the token that Vault stores in the audit log as the secret value of the token.

stem: A scheduler creates a token for each job and stores only the accessor. Which TWO actions can it perform later with just that accessor? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Read secrets on behalf of the job by presenting the accessor as the client token.
Revoke the token when the job completes, using `vault token revoke -accessor <accessor>`.
Add new policies to the existing token by supplying the accessor and a policy name.
Print the original token ID again, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.
Look up the token's properties, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.

stem: A security team needs to list every active token in a Vault cluster for an audit. Which statement about this is accurate?

choices.text: The only way to list tokens is `auth/token/accessors`, which returns accessors rather than tokens.
`vault list auth/token/tokens` returns the token IDs, so auditors can reuse them to log in to Vault.
Vault cannot list tokens, so auditors must parse the audit log for token IDs.

stem: A developer reads `token_duration 768h` in the output of `vault token create` and asks what the TTL of a Vault service token actually describes. Which is accurate?

choices.text: The time since the token's last use, after which Vault revokes it as inactive.
The total lifetime from creation that can never be extended, no matter how often it is renewed.
The number of times the token can be used before Vault revokes it automatically.
The period of validity since the token's creation or its last renewal, whichever is more recent.

stem: A service token was created with a 1 hour TTL, and the application renews it every 30 minutes. After several weeks a renewal returns a TTL shorter than requested, and later the token stops working. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The 30 minute interval is shorter than the TTL, so Vault treats it as abusive and stops extending.
The token became an orphan, and orphan tokens cannot be renewed after one day.
The token reached the maximum TTL that applies to it, so renewals can no longer extend it.
Vault revokes any token that is renewed more than 48 times in a row.

stem: A token is created with `vault token create -ttl=1h -explicit-max-ttl=4h`. The application renews it each hour. How long can this token live in total?

choices.text: Thirty-two days, because the system max TTL replaces an explicit max TTL.
Indefinitely, because renewing before expiry resets the explicit max TTL each time.
Four hours, because the explicit max TTL is a hard limit that renewals cannot extend.
One hour, because the explicit max TTL applies only if the token is not renewed.

stem: A long-running service keeps a database connection pool and must not lose its Vault token while it is alive, but the token should expire soon after the service is shut down. Which TWO statements about using a periodic token for this are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: If the service stops renewing, the token expires within the period, and its leases are revoked.
Periodic tokens are batch tokens, so renewals are performed by the service without storage.

stem: A client received a `403` with `invalid token` and `permission denied` messages when calling Vault with a token that worked yesterday. The token has a 24 hour TTL and was never renewed. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The policy attached to the token was deleted, which turns every call into an invalid token response.
Vault was sealed and unsealed overnight, and sealing deletes all service tokens.
The client IP changed, and Vault answers an unknown source address with `invalid token`.
The token passed its TTL, so Vault revoked it and rejects it as invalid.

stem: During a design review the team debates whether to use orphan tokens for long-lived integrations. Which statement about orphan tokens is accurate?

choices.text: An orphan token is a token whose parent has expired, so Vault immediately revokes it.
An orphan token has no parent, so it is the root of its own tree and is not revoked with other tokens.
An orphan token is a root token without an expiration, created once at `vault operator init` time.
An orphan token can only be a batch token, because service tokens always have a parent.

stem: An engineer logged in with `vault login -method=userpass username=alice` and then ran `vault token create -policy=app` from that session. Later Alice's session token is revoked with `vault token revoke -self`. What happens to the `app` token?

choices.text: It keeps working, because tokens created with `-policy` are always orphans.
Vault revokes it too, because it is a child of the revoked session token.
It keeps working, because only the leases of the parent are revoked.

stem: A team rotates the token of a deployment service every day by revoking the old token. Each time, tokens created earlier by that service for other apps stop working and the apps fail. Which change fixes this without changing what the apps are allowed to do?

choices.text: Change the app tokens to batch tokens, which are unaffected by revoking a parent.
Increase the service token's TTL so that the old token is never revoked.
Attach the `root` policy to the app tokens so that they do not depend on the service.
Have the service create the app tokens as orphans, using a role with `orphan` enabled or `create-orphan`.

stem: A platform engineer is reviewing how tokens end up without a parent in a Vault cluster. Which TWO actions create an orphan token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Writing to `auth/token/create-orphan` with a token whose policy allows it.
Running `vault token create -use-limit=1` with an ordinary child token.
Running `vault token create -policy=app` with a token that is allowed to create child tokens.

stem: A team wants a token for a scheduler that must have only the `batch-jobs` policy, with no `default` policy. Which command creates it?

stem: A team plans to standardize token creation for CI jobs by defining a token store role named `ci`. Which statement about token store roles is accurate?

Performance standbys, which cache the root key in memory after the first successful unseal
Disaster recovery replication, which keeps the secondary unsealed with the primary's KMS key

stem: A Vault Enterprise customer needs a warm standby cluster in another region. After a regional outage, applications should keep their existing tokens and leases with no new logins. Which replication type fits?

choices.text: Performance replication, since secondaries keep their own tokens and leases for local clients
Disaster recovery replication, since the secondary shares the primary's token and lease data and is promoted on failure
Performance replication, since secondaries mirror local mounts and tokens from the primary
Disaster recovery replication, since the secondary serves client reads while the primary is healthy

stem: A Vault Enterprise company in the United States wants application servers in Asia to read KV and use transit with low latency, while one primary cluster stays the system of record. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A disaster recovery secondary in Asia, so that local applications read from it while the primary is healthy
More standby nodes in the U.S. cluster, because standbys in the same cluster reduce intercontinental latency
A performance secondary in Asia, which serves local requests and forwards writes to shared state to the primary
A second standalone cluster in Asia with its own KV data, synchronised by running the same CLI commands twice

stem: A Vault Enterprise team enabled a KV mount on a performance primary with the `-local` flag. Engineers in the secondary region cannot see this mount. Which statement explains it?

choices.text: Local mounts need a paths filter on the secondary before the data can be read there
Local mounts are replicated to performance secondaries, but only after the next snapshot
Local mounts are deleted on every secondary when the primary is promoted
Local mounts replicate only to disaster recovery secondaries, so a performance secondary never sees them

stem: A primary Vault Enterprise cluster in the EU holds a namespace with regulated customer data. A performance secondary in another region must not receive it. Which feature controls this?

choices.text: A paths filter on the secondary that excludes the namespace or mount path from replication
A longer lease TTL on the namespace, so secondaries cannot refresh the data
A DR secondary token, because DR clusters accept only data that is explicitly allowed
The seal wrap setting, which hides the namespace from secondaries that lack the KMS key

stem: The link between a performance secondary and its primary drops for ten minutes. A client of the secondary reads a KV secret and then tries to write a new KV secret. What happens?

choices.text: Both fail, because a disconnected secondary seals itself until it contacts the primary
The read succeeds with possibly stale data, while the write fails as it cannot reach the primary
Both succeed; the write is queued and delivered to the primary when the link returns
The read fails and the write succeeds, because writes are stored on the secondary first

stem: An engineer activates replication on a new secondary that uses a Shamir seal, where the primary also uses a Shamir seal. What happens to the secondary's seal configuration?

choices.text: It switches automatically to auto-unseal, using the primary's KMS configuration
It keeps its own unseal keys, and the primary's keys are added as extra recovery keys
It is unchanged, since replication copies only data and never touches seals
It is replaced with the primary's Shamir configuration and unseal keys

stem: Which TWO statements correctly compare self-managed Vault Enterprise with a HashiCorp-managed HCP Vault Dedicated cluster? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A self-managed cluster is always on Integrated Storage, while HCP Vault Dedicated lets you pick Consul
Self-managed clusters are upgraded automatically, while HCP Vault Dedicated clusters wait for the customer
HCP Vault Dedicated uses auto-unseal with a unique KMS key per cluster, managed by HashiCorp
Customers of HCP Vault Dedicated manage the HSM used for auto-unseal in the same way as self-managed users
HCP Vault Dedicated is operated by HashiCorp, which handles backups, upgrades and platform recovery

stem: A team moves from a self-managed cluster to a HashiCorp-managed HCP Vault Dedicated cluster. At first login, how do administrators get a highly privileged token, and where do their namespaces start?

choices.text: They use the shared root token stored in the HashiCorp support portal after submitting an unseal request
They read the initial root token from the init output and create namespaces under the `root` namespace
They run `vault operator init` on the cluster, and the top-level namespace is `root`
They generate an admin token from the HCP Portal, and the top-level namespace is `admin`

stem: A new engineer asks how Vault protects the data it writes to storage. Which statement about the key chain is accurate?

choices.text: The unseal key encrypts the root key, the root key encrypts the encryption key, and the encryption key encrypts the stored data
The unseal key encrypts the stored data directly, and the root key is only used to sign tokens that clients present to Vault
The root key encrypts the stored data, and the unseal key is a copy of the root key that is kept in the storage backend
The encryption key encrypts the root key, the root key encrypts the unseal key, and the unseal key encrypts each secret

stem: A security reviewer asks what the Vault security barrier does for data on its way to the storage backend. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It hashes each object with SHA-256 before writing it, so a modified object is detected but its content is stored readable
It encrypts every object with AES-256-GCM before it leaves Vault and checks the authentication tag when the object is read back
It relies on the storage backend to encrypt data at rest, and adds TLS only between Vault and the backend
It encrypts only values marked as sensitive by the secrets engine and leaves path names and policies in plaintext in storage

stem: An attacker copies a full snapshot of the storage backend files from a stopped Vault node. The attacker has no unseal keys and no Vault token. What can the attacker read?

choices.text: All secrets in plaintext, once the attacker replays stored token records against the sealed server
Only the names of auth methods, because those are intentionally stored unencrypted for use during unseal
Only encrypted data; the encryption key and root key are stored encrypted and cannot be decrypted without the unseal key
All secrets in plaintext, because the node's storage files are readable with filesystem access

stem: Which TWO statements about the root key and the encryption key are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The root key is stored in the storage backend, encrypted by the unseal key
The root key is generated at every unseal and is never written to any storage
The encryption key is reconstructed from the Shamir shares given to operators
The root key is the same value as the initial root token printed during initialization
The encryption key is kept in the keyring and encrypts most of the data Vault stores

stem: An operator wants to know where the plaintext root key exists while a node is running. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It exists in the client token cache at `~/.vault-token` on the machine of the operator who unsealed
It is written to a file under the Vault data directory so that a restarted node can read it automatically
It exists only in the memory of the unsealed node, and `vault operator seal` discards it from memory
It is kept in memory on every node of the cluster permanently, whether sealed or unsealed

stem: What does `vault operator init` accomplish on a brand-new Vault server?

choices.text: It unseals the server for the first time, using shares that it reads from the configuration file
It prepares storage for data, generates the root key, and returns the key shares and an initial root token
It creates the first KV secrets engine mount and a policy that grants the operator full access
It copies the data of a peer node into the new server so both hold the same secrets

stem: Three Vault servers share one storage backend in an HA cluster. Node 1 was initialized and unsealed. An operator now runs `vault operator init` against node 2. What happens?

choices.text: The command succeeds and generates a second set of key shares that either node can use
The command succeeds only if the operator first runs `vault operator seal` on node 1
The command succeeds and replaces the earlier shares, which invalidates the keys of node 1
The command fails because the cluster is already initialized; node 2 only needs to be unsealed

stem: A provisioning script must decide whether to run `vault operator init` and wants to use only exit codes. Which command and result fit?

choices.text: `vault status` returns exit code 0 when Vault is not yet initialized
`vault operator init -status` returns exit code 2 when Vault is not initialized
`vault operator init -status` returns exit code 0 when Vault is not initialized
`vault operator init -status` returns exit code 1 when Vault is not initialized

stem: Which TWO statements about the default behavior of `vault operator init` are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It splits the key into 3 shares and requires all 3 shares
It prints no root token and expects one to be generated later
It requires the operator to name a PGP key for each share
It requires 3 of the shares to reconstruct the key
It splits the unseal key into 5 key shares

stem: An on-call engineer holds a token whose only policy is `path "sys/seal" { capabilities = ["update"] }`. During an incident they run `vault operator seal` against the active node. What happens?

The command succeeds, but only after the engineer supplies the threshold of unseal shares at a prompt
The command is refused with permission denied, because sealing needs the root policy or the sudo capability on the path

stem: Policy requires that nobody sees plaintext key shares or the initial root token on the init output. Which command meets it?

`vault operator init -key-shares=3 -key-threshold=2 -pgp-keys="keybase:ann,keybase:bo"`, which encrypts the shares

stem: A monitoring probe hits a Vault node that was just restarted and is sealed. Which TWO operations can the node still perform? (Select TWO)

Serving transit encrypt requests with cached keys, but creating no new mounts
Logging in with auth methods and issuing tokens, but returning no secret values
Reading secrets from KV mounts created before the restart, since the data is still in storage
Accepting unseal key shares through `vault operator unseal`

stem: A cluster uses a Shamir seal. An application logged in earlier today. After an unplanned restart of a node, `vault kv get secret/app` returns an error that Vault is sealed. Which action restores service?

Supply the threshold of unseal shares with `vault operator unseal`; data and tokens are served again
Run `vault operator init` again so that the node generates a new root key

stem: Which TWO events return an unsealed Vault node to the sealed state? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The initial root token is revoked
An auth method is disabled
All dynamic secret leases expire
The Vault process is restarted
An operator with root privileges calls the seal API or runs `vault operator seal`

stem: Which statement about who may seal a Vault server is accurate?

choices.text: It requires the threshold of unseal shares, entered with the `vault operator seal` command
Sealing is possible only through the UI, because the CLI cannot seal a server
A single operator with root privileges can seal, while unsealing needs the share threshold
Sealing needs two operators with the same policy, much like generating a root token

stem: Two of three required unseal shares have been entered when intrusion detection fires. The on-call operator runs `vault operator seal`. What is the effect on the unseal in progress?

The two entered shares are kept, and one more share completes the unseal later
The seal command is rejected because an unseal is in progress
The unseal progress is reset, and the shares must be entered again from the beginning

stem: An operator typed `vault operator unseal <share>` and saw the same share go to the shell history. Which approach is recommended for entering shares?

choices.text: Write all shares to one file and pass the file path with `-key-file`
Run `vault operator unseal` with no argument so it prompts for the key with hidden input
Export the share in an environment variable named `VAULT_UNSEAL_KEY`, which the CLI reads automatically
Pass the share with `-format=json` so that the command redacts it in the history

stem: An operator entered a wrong share in a threshold of three and now doubts the earlier entries. Which command discards the shares entered so far so that the process starts again?

choices.text: `vault operator init -status`, which prints and clears the pending entries
`vault operator unseal -migrate`, which discards earlier shares and starts a fresh count
`vault operator unseal -reset`
`vault status -reset`

stem: A Shamir-sealed node has a threshold of three. Three operators each enter one share against this same node from three different workstations, with no shared session between them. What is the result?

choices.text: The node unseals when the third share arrives, because the server itself holds the progress between submissions
The node stays sealed, because each submission from a different client resets the unseal progress counter
The node stays sealed, because every share must be entered from one client machine in the same session
The node unseals only if all three submissions carry the same client token in the request header

stem: A deployment script runs `vault status` and branches on the exit code. Which mapping is accurate?

choices.text: 0 means unsealed, 1 means sealed, 2 means an error occurred
0 means initialized, 1 means unsealed, 2 means an error occurred
0 means unsealed, 1 means an error occurred, 2 means sealed
0 means sealed, 1 means unsealed, 2 means not initialized

stem: On a freshly started server with an empty data directory, `vault status` shows `Initialized false` and `Sealed true`. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The node needs only `vault login` with the root token to leave sealed state
Run `vault operator init` first, then supply the threshold of shares to unseal
The node is sealed by an attack, and `vault operator unseal -reset` restores it
The operator can unseal first with any random keys, then initialize the server

stem: The CLI on a laptop prints a connection error to `https://127.0.0.1:8200`, but the Vault server runs at `https://vault.corp.example:8200`. What is the cleanest fix for all later commands in this shell?

Run `export VAULT_TOKEN="https://vault.corp.example:8200"` so the token names the server
Run `vault operator init` so the CLI learns the server address
Run `export VAULT_ADDR="https://vault.corp.example:8200"` once in the shell

stem: Which TWO statements about the CLI settings for trusting a server certificate are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `VAULT_CAPATH` holds the path of a directory that contains PEM-encoded CA certificate files
Setting `VAULT_CAPATH` switches off verification of the server certificate until the variable is unset
`VAULT_CACERT` and `VAULT_CAPATH` are read by the server process to decide which clients it trusts
`VAULT_CAPATH` holds the path of a single DER-encoded certificate that is sent to the server as a client certificate
`VAULT_CACERT` holds the path of one PEM-encoded CA certificate file and takes precedence over `VAULT_CAPATH`

stem: A developer sets `VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=1` in a shell profile on a laptop that connects to the production Vault. Which statement about this setting is accurate?

It disables TLS entirely, so the CLI talks to Vault over plain HTTP

stem: An engineer exports `VAULT_TOKEN` in a shell and then runs `vault kv get secret/app` without calling `vault login`. What does the CLI do?
